subject: Climate & Environment
title: De-Extinction: Bringing Species Back
description: A 60-second lesson on De-Extinction: Bringing Species Back.

hook.text: Scientists are working to resurrect the woolly mammoth using gene editing. Is it a good idea?

buildup.text: CRISPR can insert mammoth genes — cold resistance, thick hair — into Asian elephant DNA.

discovery.text: The goal isn't a perfect clone but a cold-adapted elephant that could restore tundra grasslands.

twist.text: Critics argue de-extinction diverts money from protecting species that still exist.

climax.text: The technology also applies to recently extinct species like the Christmas Island rat.

punchline.text: Resurrection is possible. Preventing extinction is still easier.

quiz.question: What technology is being used for de-extinction efforts?

details.summary: De-extinction aims to resurrect vanished species using genetic technologies such as gene editing, cloning, and selective breeding. Projects target the woolly mammoth, passenger pigeon, and thylacine, but ethical, ecological, and practical challenges remain formidable.
details.whyItMatters: De-extinction raises profound questions about whether technology should try to undo past losses and whether resources are better spent preventing current extinctions.
takeaways: CRISPR gene editing could insert extinct species' traits into living relatives
No species has been fully resurrected from extinction yet
Critics warn de-extinction diverts funding from protecting living species

faq.question: How close are scientists to bringing back the woolly mammoth?
faq.answer: Colossal Biosciences is editing Asian elephant DNA to incorporate mammoth cold-adapted traits. The goal is a mammoth-like hybrid, not a genetic replica. Producing a viable embryo faces major surrogacy and developmental challenges with no definite timeline.

faq.question: Would de-extinct species survive in the wild?
faq.answer: Survival is uncertain. The habitats many extinct species lived in have changed dramatically. A resurrected species may lack learned behaviors, face new diseases, and find no ecological niche, raising questions about whether release is responsible.
